The Ship of Theseus Explained and Why It Matters for Data Modeling

Released Feb 18, 2026, 22 min

Play The Ship of Theseus Explained and Why It Matters for Data Modeling on YouTube
Watch on YouTube

I had to replace my car’s transmission… but somehow it’s still the same car.

Is it really?

In this episode we dive into one of the oldest and strangest puzzles in metaphysics: the Ship of Theseus. Starting with the legend of Theseus, recorded by Plutarch and later expanded by Thomas Hobbes, we ask a deceptively simple question: if you replace something piece by piece, is it still the same thing?

We explore numerical versus qualitative identity, Leibniz’s Law, essential versus accidental properties, and persistence conditions. Along the way we see why every metaphysical theory sounds completely reasonable at first and then totally crazy once you follow it through.

But this is not just ivory tower philosophy. These same problems show up in ontology engineering, data modeling, defining what counts as a vehicle, deciding whether a VIN determines identity, and resolving messy real world data. Even sports franchises raise identity puzzles, like whether the Seattle SuperSonics are the same team as the Oklahoma City Thunder.

Every schema quietly commits you to a metaphysics. What kinds of things exist? Which properties are essential? When does something stop being the same object?

If you build databases, knowledge graphs, or ontologies, you are already doing metaphysics whether you realize it or not.

By the end, you will have practical philosophical tools to think more clearly about identity, persistence, and entity resolution in your own systems.
